# Kessford Community Archive: from index cards to search by street

How we helped a volunteer-run archive get its photographs online and searchable in ten weeks, on a £9,000 budget, using the library's existing website.

Kessford Community Archive lives in a back room of Kessford Library. Its 14 regular volunteers, most of them retired, look after about 3,400 photographs of the town, from the 1890s to the 1990s. Until this year, the catalogue was a set of handwritten index cards, and the only way to search it was to come in on a Tuesday or a Thursday and ask.

## The brief, and the limits

The archive wanted two things: its photographs online and searchable, and an online form for booking the reading room.

The limits were tight. We had £9,000 and about ten weeks, from 23 March to 3 June 2026. Everything had to run on the library's existing website system, so we couldn't install anything new. The volunteers would do all the data entry, and many of them weren't confident with computers. And the cards themselves were uneven: the captions were inconsistent, and a lot of the photos had no date, or only a guess.

Each of those limits shaped what we built.

## Designing for the people doing the typing

We designed a catalogue entry form with six fields, then watched three volunteers use the first version. They typed everything in capitals, because the old cards were in capitals. We didn't ask them to break the habit. We changed the form, so that it accepts capitals and tidies them up. It's a small change, and it came from watching.

We ran two training sessions in the archive room itself, and wrote a one-page guide that sits next to the computer.

## Search by street

We built search around the town's streets, which gives people a way into the collection that doesn't depend on dates. That meant compiling a list of 212 street names, including 31 that have since been renamed, so a search for Chapel Row also finds the photos filed under its old name, Tanner's Lane.

For people searching in the reading room, we designed a printed leaflet explaining how it works.

## What we left out

Two things didn't make it. We'd planned a filter by decade, but we dropped it before launch, because too many of the photos had no reliable date. And the reading room booking form was cut, because the library's system couldn't support it. Bookings are still taken by phone.

Both cuts came from the same place: building for the collection and the system as they are, rather than as we'd like them to be.

## Where it stands

The collection went online on 3 June 2026, with 1,900 of the 3,400 photographs catalogued. For the first time, those photographs can be searched without coming in on a Tuesday or a Thursday. The volunteers are adding the rest at their own pace, and there's no end date.

Nadia Pell, the archive's volunteer coordinator, puts it like this: "It's the first system we've had that the volunteers don't need me standing over them to use. That's not nothing."

# The Damp of '87

When Mum moved into Elm Court last spring, the hardest thing to deal with was her piano. It was an upright my grandad bought second-hand in 1961, and it had been in the front room at Lark Road my whole life. Mum played it every Sunday, mostly hymns. The D above middle C stuck. She always said that was "the damp of '87", and none of us ever got round to fixing it.

I was sad and guilty and cross all at once. I rang three dealers and none of them were interested. One of them said they're all firewood now. I suppose I felt like nobody understood what it meant to us.

In the end I put it on the local selling page, free to a good home, buyer collects, and a man rang that evening. He came on the Saturday with his daughter, who looked about fourteen, in a van he'd borrowed from work. She sat down with her coat still on and played a scale, and of course the D stuck. I told her about the damp of '87, and she laughed.

I had to go into the kitchen for a minute.

Getting it out was a whole saga. Her dad had to take the front door off its hinges, and it took the three of us nearly an hour to get it down the steps. Before they left, he gave me two twenty-pound notes, folded up small, even though the advert said free. I tried to give them back, but he wouldn't have it.

I stood on the pavement for a long time afterwards, drained, and strangely at peace.

I kept the stool. Her music was still inside it: the Sunday hymn book, and a book of film themes I never once heard her play.

The next time I visited Mum, I was nervous about telling her. I needn't have been. All she said was, "Did the D stick?"

I said yes, and she laughed, properly, for the first time in months.

# Low Water

Skerrow is a small tidal island, joined to the mainland by a causeway that floods twice a day. It has one café. Nell Achterberg, 61, has run it alone since her husband, Piet, died two winters ago. Above the counter hangs a tide clock that Piet set twenty minutes fast, so that visitors would always leave in good time. Nell has never corrected it.

On the afternoon low tide, her daughter Ros, 29, a junior doctor in the city, walks in without warning. She hasn't been back since the funeral. Nell looks at her for a long moment, then hands her a tea towel.

The café is still busy with the day's last walkers, and Ros finds herself working. Frank, a regular who walks over every afternoon for a scone, asks her to look at his knee; she diagnoses it as seventy-four years old. Nell charges Ros for her tea. Every so often Nell glances at the clock and sends a table on its way. On Skerrow, everyone does what the clock says. Frank is the last to leave. "Clock's never wrong," Nell tells him.

Alone, the two women clear up and talk about everything except Piet. His reading glasses are still by the till. The specials board is still in his handwriting. Ros wants to be asked why she has come. Nell, who has kept going by never stopping, wants her gone before either of them has to say anything. When Ros asks how she's managing, Nell says "Fine" in exactly the voice Ros uses on patients' relatives. Then Nell looks at the clock and tells her she'll want to be off, if she's going to make her shift.

Ros puts on her coat. At the door she looks up at the clock and says, "It's twenty minutes fast." Piet told her when she was ten, and swore her to secrecy: it was for the tourists. Nell realises Ros has known all afternoon that she was being hurried out, and has let herself be hurried.

Ros takes her coat off and sits down. They have twenty minutes.

In them, Nell finally asks why she came. Ros tells her she has driven to the causeway twice since the funeral and turned back both times. Today she didn't, and she can't say why. Nell tells her why she has never corrected the clock: it is the last thing in the café that is still Piet's job. Neither of them cries for long. Nell makes two more teas and, this time, doesn't charge.

When the real time comes, Ros walks back across the causeway, in good time, with the sea still well out on either side. Nell watches from the window until Ros reaches the far end and turns to wave.

Back inside, Nell looks up at the clock, and leaves it exactly as it is.

# LOW WATER

Skerrow is a small tidal island, reached by a causeway that floods twice a day. Its only café belongs to Nell Achterberg, 61, who has run it alone since her husband, Piet, died two winters ago. Above the counter hangs a tide clock, with Piet's pencil line marking when the causeway closes. He set the clock twenty minutes fast, so that visitors would always leave in good time. Nell has never corrected it.

On the afternoon low tide, Nell's daughter, Ros, 29, a junior doctor in the city, walks across the causeway without warning. She hasn't been back since the funeral. Nell, pouring tea for a table of walkers, looks at her for a long moment and hands her an apron.

So the reunion happens between orders. Ros still knows where everything is kept. She's on shift at seven tomorrow, so she has to make this evening's crossing. "Then you'll go when the clock says," says Nell.

The clock runs the room. When Howard, a regular who always stays too long, asks for another pot, Nell points at it: he'll want to be off soon. Howard holds up his phone. The clock is twenty minutes fast. "It's right for here," says Nell. Ros tells him it has been fast since she was twelve, and nobody in the family has ever won that argument.

Between customers, mother and daughter circle the thing neither will name. Ros diagnoses the coffee machine: "It's got a murmur." Nell asks whether the hospital ever lets her sleep. "Not on purpose." They are good at being funny, and it saves them from talking.

The café empties. Howard leaves last, grumbling, in good time. Ros drags a chair to the counter to put the clock right, and Nell tells her to leave it. It becomes the argument they have both avoided, and Ros finally says it. At Piet's wake she left before it was over. She said she had to catch the tide, looked up at this clock, knew it was fast, and went anyway. She has been ashamed of it for two winters.

Nell says she knows. She watched her go. She has been waiting ever since for Ros to walk back in, and never knew how to say so on the phone.

The clock's hand touches Piet's pencil line. Ros stands and reaches for her coat, just as she did at the wake.

"Sit down," says Nell. "The clock's for visitors. You're not a visitor."

Ros sits. Nell gives her ten of Piet's twenty minutes, because he would want the other ten kept, and for the first time all day she sits down too. They don't say much. They share the last scone.

Then Ros crosses in good time, with the causeway dry and the sea still well out. Nell watches from the window until her daughter reaches the far side. Above the counter, the clock keeps its twenty minutes, as it always has.

# Kessford Community Archive: from index cards to search by street

*An online photo catalogue for a volunteer-run archive, built in ten weeks on £9,000 without installing anything new.*

We watched three volunteers try the first version of our catalogue entry form. All three typed everything in capitals, because the old index cards were in capitals. So we changed the form to accept capitals and tidy them up.

Kessford Community Archive is a volunteer-run local history archive in a back room of Kessford Library. It has 14 regular volunteers, most of them retired, and about 3,400 photographs of the town from the 1890s to the 1990s. Those photographs were catalogued on handwritten index cards, and the only way to search them was to come in on a Tuesday or Thursday and ask.

The archive asked us for two things: get the photographs online and searchable, and let people book the reading room with an online form instead of by phone. The limits were tight:

- The budget was £9,000.
- We had about ten weeks, from 23 March to 3 June 2026.
- Everything had to run on the library's existing website system. We couldn't install anything new.
- The volunteers would do all the data entry, and many of them weren't confident with computers.
- The captions on the cards were inconsistent, and a lot of the photographs had no date, or only a guess.

The finished entry form has six fields. Volunteers can type the way the cards were written, and the form tidies up after them. Alongside it, we ran two training sessions in the archive room and wrote a one-page guide that sits next to the computer.

Search works by street. We compiled a list of 212 street names, including 31 that have since been renamed, so a search for Chapel Row also finds the photographs filed under its old name, Tanner's Lane. For people who come in, we designed a printed leaflet for the reading room that explains how to search.

Two things didn't make it. We'd planned a filter by decade, and dropped it before launch because too many photographs had no reliable date. The reading room booking form was cut because the library's system couldn't support it, so bookings are still made by phone.

The catalogue launched on 3 June 2026 with 1,900 of the 3,400 photographs online, where nobody has to wait for a Tuesday or a Thursday to search them. The volunteers are adding the rest at their own pace, and there's no end date.

Nadia Pell, the archive's volunteer coordinator, puts it like this: "It's the first system we've had that the volunteers don't need me standing over them to use. That's not nothing."

# LOW WATER

Afternoon low tide on Skerrow, a small island reached by a causeway that floods twice a day. In the island's only café, NELL ACHTERBERG (61) is moving the last walkers along. One of them, a WALKER in a new waterproof, asks for another pot of tea. Nell points at the tide clock above the counter. He checks the tide times on his phone and says he has time. "The clock's right," says Nell. He goes.

It isn't. Nell's husband, Piet, set it twenty minutes fast so that visitors would always leave in good time. He died two winters ago, and Nell has run the café alone since. She has never corrected the clock.

The door opens on her daughter, ROS (29), a junior doctor in the city. She hasn't been back since the funeral, and she hasn't said she was coming. "I was passing," she says. "Nobody passes Skerrow," says Nell, and hands her a tea towel.

Ros dries cups while the last tables empty. She's on shift at 7am tomorrow, so she has to make this evening's crossing. Nell looks up at the clock and tells her when to leave by it. Ros checks the tide times on her phone, and lets it go.

With the café empty, they talk around Piet. Ros asks why the clock still hasn't been put right. "It isn't wrong," says Nell. "It's early." "Chronically," says Ros. Nell mentions that the spare bed is made up. Ros says she's on at seven. Nell says the hospital must have other doctors. "Not spare ones," says Ros.

Ros sits in the window seat to finish her tea, and within a minute she is asleep in her coat, the mug tilting in her hand. Nell takes the mug.

The clock's hand creeps towards the time Nell gave her. Every visitor for two winters has been sent off by that clock. Nell drags a chair to the counter, climbs up, and moves the hand back twenty minutes. For the first time since Piet set it, the clock is right.

She sits down opposite her sleeping daughter and does nothing at all for twenty minutes.

Then she wakes her. Ros looks up at the clock, then at the tide times on her phone. They agree. She looks at her mother. Neither of them says a word about it.

Ros walks the causeway without hurrying. The sand is firm, and the water is still a long way off on both sides. Halfway across, she turns. Nell is standing in the café doorway. Behind her, above the counter, the clock shows the true tide.

# The Damp of '87

When Mum moved into Elm Court last spring, the hardest thing to deal with was her piano. It was an upright my grandad bought second-hand in 1961, and it had been in the front room at Lark Road my whole life. Mum played it every Sunday, mostly hymns. She always said the D above middle C stuck because of 'the damp of '87', and none of us ever got round to fixing it.

I rang three dealers and none of them were interested. One of them said they're all firewood now. I suppose I felt like nobody understood what it meant to us.

In the end I put it on the local selling page, free to a good home, buyer collects, and a man rang that evening. He came on the Saturday with his daughter, who looked about fourteen, in a van he'd borrowed from work. She sat down with her coat still on and played a scale, and of course the D stuck. I told her about the damp of '87 and she laughed. I had to go into the kitchen for a minute.

Getting it out was a whole saga. Her dad had to take the front door off its hinges, and it took the three of us nearly an hour to get it down the steps. Before they left he gave me two twenty-pound notes, folded up small, even though the advert said free. I tried to give them back but he wouldn't have it. I stood on the pavement for a long time afterwards, strangely at peace.

I kept the stool. Her music was still inside it: the Sunday hymn book, and a book of film themes I never once heard her play.

The next time I visited Mum, I was nervous about telling her, but I needn't have been. All she said was, 'Did the D stick?'

I said yes, and she laughed properly for the first time in months.

In March last year, I spent a week in the main entrance at Orla Valley, standing by the reception desk with a clipboard.

Five days, from eight in the morning till six at night. I wrote down every question people asked the two receptionists.

By the end of the week, I had thirteen hundred and twelve questions.

Three hundred and ninety of them were some version of the same question. "Where's X-ray?"

The sign over the main corridor said "Imaging and Radiology". It had said "Imaging and Radiology" since the building opened, in two thousand and nine. There wasn't a single sign, anywhere in the hospital, that said "X-ray".

# Kessford Community Archive: from index cards to search by street

How we helped a volunteer-run archive get its photographs online and searchable in ten weeks, on a £9,000 budget, using the library's existing website.

Kessford Community Archive lives in a back room of Kessford Library. Its 14 regular volunteers, most of them retired, look after about 3,400 photographs of the town, from the 1890s to the 1990s. Until this year, the catalogue was a set of handwritten index cards, and the only way to search it was to come in on a Tuesday or a Thursday and ask.

## The brief, and the limits

The archive wanted two things: its photographs online and searchable, and an online form for booking the reading room.

The limits were tight. We had £9,000 and about ten weeks, from 23 March to 3 June 2026. Everything had to run on the library's existing website system, so we couldn't install anything new. The volunteers would do all the data entry, and many of them weren't confident with computers. And the cards themselves were uneven: the captions were inconsistent, and a lot of the photos had no date, or only a guess.

Each of those limits shaped what we built.

## Designing for the people doing the typing

We designed a catalogue entry form with six fields, then watched three volunteers use the first version. They typed everything in capitals, because the old cards were in capitals. We didn't ask them to break the habit. We changed the form, so that it accepts capitals and tidies them up. It's a small change, and it came from watching.

We ran two training sessions in the archive room itself, and wrote a one-page guide that sits next to the computer.

## Search by street

We built search around the town's streets, which gives people a way into the collection that doesn't depend on dates. That meant compiling a list of 212 street names, including 31 that have since been renamed, so a search for Chapel Row also finds the photos filed under its old name, Tanner's Lane.

For people searching in the reading room, we designed a printed leaflet explaining how it works.

## What we left out

Two things didn't make it. We'd planned a filter by decade, but we dropped it before launch, because too many of the photos had no reliable date. And the reading room booking form was cut, because the library's system couldn't support it. Bookings are still taken by phone.

Both cuts came from the same place: building for the collection and the system as they are, rather than as we'd like them to be.

## Where it stands

The collection went online on 3 June 2026, with 1,900 of the 3,400 photographs catalogued. For the first time, those photographs can be searched without coming in on a Tuesday or a Thursday. The volunteers are adding the rest at their own pace, and there's no end date.

Nadia Pell, the archive's volunteer coordinator, puts it like this: "It's the first system we've had that the volunteers don't need me standing over them to use. That's not nothing."

# Low Water

Skerrow is a small tidal island, joined to the mainland by a causeway that floods twice a day. It has one café. Nell Achterberg, 61, has run it alone since her husband, Piet, died two winters ago. Above the counter hangs a tide clock that Piet set twenty minutes fast, so that visitors would always leave in good time. Nell has never corrected it.

On the afternoon low tide, her daughter Ros, 29, a junior doctor in the city, walks in without warning. She hasn't been back since the funeral. Nell looks at her for a long moment, then hands her a tea towel.

The café is still busy with the day's last walkers, and Ros finds herself working. Frank, a regular who walks over every afternoon for a scone, asks her to look at his knee; she diagnoses it as seventy-four years old. Nell charges Ros for her tea. Every so often Nell glances at the clock and sends a table on its way. On Skerrow, everyone does what the clock says. Frank is the last to leave. "Clock's never wrong," Nell tells him.

Alone, the two women clear up and talk about everything except Piet. His reading glasses are still by the till. The specials board is still in his handwriting. Ros wants to be asked why she has come. Nell, who has kept going by never stopping, wants her gone before either of them has to say anything. When Ros asks how she's managing, Nell says "Fine" in exactly the voice Ros uses on patients' relatives. Then Nell looks at the clock and tells her she'll want to be off, if she's going to make her shift.

Ros puts on her coat. At the door she looks up at the clock and says, "It's twenty minutes fast." Piet told her when she was ten, and swore her to secrecy: it was for the tourists. Nell realises Ros has known all afternoon that she was being hurried out, and has let herself be hurried.

Ros takes her coat off and sits down. They have twenty minutes.

In them, Nell finally asks why she came. Ros tells her she has driven to the causeway twice since the funeral and turned back both times. Today she didn't, and she can't say why. Nell tells her why she has never corrected the clock: it is the last thing in the café that is still Piet's job. Neither of them cries for long. Nell makes two more teas and, this time, doesn't charge.

When the real time comes, Ros walks back across the causeway, in good time, with the sea still well out on either side. Nell watches from the window until Ros reaches the far end and turns to wave.

Back inside, Nell looks up at the clock, and leaves it exactly as it is.

# LOW WATER

Afternoon low tide on Skerrow, a small island reached by a causeway that floods twice a day. In the island's only café, NELL ACHTERBERG (61) is moving the last walkers along. One of them, a WALKER in a new waterproof, asks for another pot of tea. Nell points at the tide clock above the counter. He checks the tide times on his phone and says he has time. "The clock's right," says Nell. He goes.

It isn't. Nell's husband, Piet, set it twenty minutes fast so that visitors would always leave in good time. He died two winters ago, and Nell has run the café alone since. She has never corrected the clock.

The door opens on her daughter, ROS (29), a junior doctor in the city. She hasn't been back since the funeral, and she hasn't said she was coming. "I was passing," she says. "Nobody passes Skerrow," says Nell, and hands her a tea towel.

Ros dries cups while the last tables empty. She's on shift at 7am tomorrow, so she has to make this evening's crossing. Nell looks up at the clock and tells her when to leave by it. Ros checks the tide times on her phone, and lets it go.

With the café empty, they talk around Piet. Ros asks why the clock still hasn't been put right. "It isn't wrong," says Nell. "It's early." "Chronically," says Ros. Nell mentions that the spare bed is made up. Ros says she's on at seven. Nell says the hospital must have other doctors. "Not spare ones," says Ros.

Ros sits in the window seat to finish her tea, and within a minute she is asleep in her coat, the mug tilting in her hand. Nell takes the mug.

The clock's hand creeps towards the time Nell gave her. Every visitor for two winters has been sent off by that clock. Nell drags a chair to the counter, climbs up, and moves the hand back twenty minutes. For the first time since Piet set it, the clock is right.

She sits down opposite her sleeping daughter and does nothing at all for twenty minutes.

Then she wakes her. Ros looks up at the clock, then at the tide times on her phone. They agree. She looks at her mother. Neither of them says a word about it.

Ros walks the causeway without hurrying. The sand is firm, and the water is still a long way off on both sides. Halfway across, she turns. Nell is standing in the café doorway. Behind her, above the counter, the clock shows the true tide.

In March last year, I spent a week at the main entrance of Orla Valley Hospital. I stood by the reception desk with a clipboard. Five days, eight in the morning until six at night. Every time someone asked one of our two receptionists a question, I wrote it down.

By the end of the week, I had thirteen hundred and twelve questions.

Three hundred and ninety of them were some version of the same question.

Where's X-ray?

On the Friday evening, I counted the signs in our main corridor. There were two hundred and fourteen. Not one of them said X-ray. There wasn't a single sign anywhere in the hospital that said X-ray.

The sign over the main corridor said Imaging and Radiology. It had said Imaging and Radiology since the building opened in 2009.

One man that week didn't ask the receptionists. He asked me. He was in a dressing gown, and he said, "Is Imaging the same as X-ray, or is that somewhere else?"

I didn't know whether it was my place to answer him.

The Monday after, we changed that one sign.

I'll come back to what happened.

Five days, eight in the morning until six at night. I wasn't there to answer anything. I was there to write down every question people asked our two receptionists.

By the end of the week, I had one thousand, three hundred and twelve questions.

Three hundred and ninety of them were some version of the same one: "Where's X-ray?"

The sign over our main corridor said "Imaging and Radiology". It had said that since the building opened in 2009. There wasn't a single sign anywhere that said "X-ray".

On the Friday evening, I counted the signs in that main corridor. There were two hundred and fourteen.

At some point that week, a man in a dressing gown came up and asked me a question. Not the receptionists. Me. He said, "Is Imaging the same as X-ray, or is that somewhere else?"

I didn't know whether it was my place to answer him.

The Monday after, we changed that one sign.

I'll come back to what happened next.

# The Damp of '87

When Mum moved into Elm Court last spring, the hardest thing to find a home for was her piano. It was an upright my grandad bought second-hand in 1961, and it had been in the front room at Lark Road my whole life. Mum played it every Sunday, mostly hymns. She always said the D above middle C stuck because of "the damp of '87", and none of us ever got round to fixing it.

I rang three dealers and none of them were interested. One of them said they're all firewood now. I suppose I felt like nobody understood what it meant to us.

In the end I put it on the local selling page, free to a good home, buyer collects, and a man rang that evening. He came on the Saturday with his daughter, who looked about fourteen, in a van he'd borrowed from work. She sat down with her coat still on and played a scale, and of course the D stuck. I told her about the damp of '87, and she laughed. I had to go into the kitchen for a minute.

Getting it out was a whole saga. Her dad had to take the front door off its hinges, and it took the three of us nearly an hour to get it down the steps. Before they left, he gave me two twenty-pound notes, folded up small, even though the advert said free. I tried to give them back, but he wouldn't have it. I stood on the pavement for a long time afterwards.

I kept the stool. Her music was still inside it: the Sunday hymn book, and a book of film themes I never once heard her play.

The next time I visited Mum, I was nervous about telling her, but I needn't have been. All she said was, "Did the D stick?"

I said yes, and she laughed properly for the first time in months.

# Pollard Street Tool Library

Calder-Wynn Foundation, Neighbourhood Resilience Fund. Panel presentation, Thursday 19 November 2026.

## Slide 1

**Headline:** Pollard Street Tool Library

**On the slide:**
In Ferrisham, members borrow tools and household equipment for a week instead of buying them.
We're asking for £36,400 over 24 months.

**Speaker note:** Thank you for having us. I'm Ines Marlow. Arjun Tate and I set the library up as a community interest company in 2024, and he's here for your questions. You've read our application and our year-one report, so I won't repeat them. I want to show you what year one taught us, and what this grant would change.

## Slide 2

**Headline:** Year one, on two volunteer sessions a week

**On the slide:**
1,146 loans.
612 items in stock, 94% of them donated.
23 active volunteers.
41% of members joined on pay what you can.

**Speaker note:** Members borrow for a week at a time. Membership is £15 a year, or pay what you can for anyone on benefits. Neither Arjun nor I is paid. All of this came from two sessions a week, Wednesday evening and Saturday, run by volunteers in a former launderette at 14 Pollard Street.

## Slide 3

**Headline:** We aimed for 500 members by March. We had 287.

**On the slide:**
Target for 31 March 2026: 500 members.
Actual: 287.
On 31 August 2026: 341.

**Speaker note:** You'll have seen this in the report, and I'd rather start with it than wait for the question. We fell well short. We've grown since, to 341 at the end of August. But growth alone doesn't deal with why we missed, and the next slide is what we think the reasons are.

## Slide 4

**Headline:** Why we think we fell short

**On the slide:**
Opened 10 weeks late: the lease was delayed.
Open for two sessions a week, all run by volunteers.
People without a car couldn't get bulky things home.

**Speaker note:** The lease delay is behind us. The other two are still how the library works today. We run two sessions a week, and we can't help anyone without a car get a carpet cleaner home. Those are the two things this grant would change.

## Slide 5

**Headline:** Two more days, run by a part-time coordinator

**On the slide:**
Now: Wednesday 5–8pm and Saturday 10am–2pm.
Adding: Tuesday and Friday, 10am–4pm, run by the coordinator with volunteers.

**Speaker note:** The new days are weekday daytimes, which we don't offer at the moment. The coordinator works two days a week for the full 24 months and runs those days alongside volunteers, so they don't rest on volunteers alone. Wednesday evenings and Saturdays carry on as they are.

## Slide 6

**Headline:** A way to get the carpet cleaner home

**On the slide:**
A second-hand electric cargo trike with a lockable box.
Deliveries within 2 miles, on Tuesdays and Fridays.

**Speaker note:** This is for the third reason. People without a car told us they couldn't get bulky things home, and the carpet cleaner is one of our most borrowed items, along with the cordless drill, the ladder and the pressure washer. The trike delivers within two miles on the two new days.

## Slide 7

**Headline:** We're asking for £36,400 over 24 months

**On the slide:**
Part-time coordinator, two days a week: £22,800
Electric cargo trike: £6,900
Volunteer training, first-aid certificates, extra insurance: £6,700
1 February 2027 to 31 January 2029

**Speaker note:** Most of the money is the coordinator, because the new days are the biggest change. The last line is what those days need: trained volunteers, first-aid certificates and the extra insurance. The grant would run from 1 February 2027, when funded projects can start, to 31 January 2029.

## Slide 8

**Headline:** After the grant: how we plan to pay the coordinator

**On the slide:**
£3 per delivery, from February 2028
Standard membership £20, from April 2028
Pay what you can: unchanged
Aim: fees cover the coordinator from February 2029
Not yet tested with members

**Speaker note:** Your guidance says panels will want to know how the work continues after the grant ends. This is our plan. Standard membership would go from £15 to £20. Both changes start while the grant is still running. And to be clear: we haven't tested whether members will accept either change, and we have no survey data.

## Slide 9

**Headline:** What this grant would change on Pollard Street

**On the slide:**
Open Tuesday, Wednesday, Friday and Saturday.
Deliveries by cargo trike within 2 miles.
£36,400 over 24 months, from 1 February 2027.

**Speaker note:** In 2024 we wrote on our website that everyone deserves access to the tools they need. Year one showed us what that takes here: being open more often, and a way to get things home. That's what we're asking you to fund. Thank you. Arjun and I are happy to take your questions.

# Kessford Community Archive: from index cards to search by street

How we helped a volunteer-run archive get its photographs online and searchable in ten weeks, on a £9,000 budget, using the library's existing website.

Kessford Community Archive lives in a back room of Kessford Library. Its 14 regular volunteers, most of them retired, look after about 3,400 photographs of the town, from the 1890s to the 1990s. Until this year, the catalogue was a set of handwritten index cards, and the only way to search it was to come in on a Tuesday or a Thursday and ask.

## The brief, and the limits

The archive wanted two things: its photographs online and searchable, and an online form for booking the reading room.

The limits were tight. We had £9,000 and about ten weeks, from 23 March to 3 June 2026. Everything had to run on the library's existing website system, so we couldn't install anything new. The volunteers would do all the data entry, and many of them weren't confident with computers. And the cards themselves were uneven: the captions were inconsistent, and a lot of the photos had no date, or only a guess.

Each of those limits shaped what we built.

## Designing for the people doing the typing

We designed a catalogue entry form with six fields, then watched three volunteers use the first version. They typed everything in capitals, because the old cards were in capitals. We didn't ask them to break the habit. We changed the form, so that it accepts capitals and tidies them up. It's a small change, and it came from watching.

We ran two training sessions in the archive room itself, and wrote a one-page guide that sits next to the computer.

## Search by street

We built search around the town's streets, which gives people a way into the collection that doesn't depend on dates. That meant compiling a list of 212 street names, including 31 that have since been renamed, so a search for Chapel Row also finds the photos filed under its old name, Tanner's Lane.

For people searching in the reading room, we designed a printed leaflet explaining how it works.

## What we left out

Two things didn't make it. We'd planned a filter by decade, but we dropped it before launch, because too many of the photos had no reliable date. And the reading room booking form was cut, because the library's system couldn't support it. Bookings are still taken by phone.

Both cuts came from the same place: building for the collection and the system as they are, rather than as we'd like them to be.

## Where it stands

The collection went online on 3 June 2026, with 1,900 of the 3,400 photographs catalogued. For the first time, those photographs can be searched without coming in on a Tuesday or a Thursday. The volunteers are adding the rest at their own pace, and there's no end date.

Nadia Pell, the archive's volunteer coordinator, puts it like this: "It's the first system we've had that the volunteers don't need me standing over them to use. That's not nothing."

# LOW WATER

Afternoon low tide on Skerrow, a small island reached by a causeway that floods twice a day. In the island's only café, NELL ACHTERBERG (61) is moving the last walkers along. One of them, a WALKER in a new waterproof, asks for another pot of tea. Nell points at the tide clock above the counter. He checks the tide times on his phone and says he has time. "The clock's right," says Nell. He goes.

It isn't. Nell's husband, Piet, set it twenty minutes fast so that visitors would always leave in good time. He died two winters ago, and Nell has run the café alone since. She has never corrected the clock.

The door opens on her daughter, ROS (29), a junior doctor in the city. She hasn't been back since the funeral, and she hasn't said she was coming. "I was passing," she says. "Nobody passes Skerrow," says Nell, and hands her a tea towel.

Ros dries cups while the last tables empty. She's on shift at 7am tomorrow, so she has to make this evening's crossing. Nell looks up at the clock and tells her when to leave by it. Ros checks the tide times on her phone, and lets it go.

With the café empty, they talk around Piet. Ros asks why the clock still hasn't been put right. "It isn't wrong," says Nell. "It's early." "Chronically," says Ros. Nell mentions that the spare bed is made up. Ros says she's on at seven. Nell says the hospital must have other doctors. "Not spare ones," says Ros.

Ros sits in the window seat to finish her tea, and within a minute she is asleep in her coat, the mug tilting in her hand. Nell takes the mug.

The clock's hand creeps towards the time Nell gave her. Every visitor for two winters has been sent off by that clock. Nell drags a chair to the counter, climbs up, and moves the hand back twenty minutes. For the first time since Piet set it, the clock is right.

She sits down opposite her sleeping daughter and does nothing at all for twenty minutes.

Then she wakes her. Ros looks up at the clock, then at the tide times on her phone. They agree. She looks at her mother. Neither of them says a word about it.

Ros walks the causeway without hurrying. The sand is firm, and the water is still a long way off on both sides. Halfway across, she turns. Nell is standing in the café doorway. Behind her, above the counter, the clock shows the true tide.

Alone, the two women clear up and talk about everything except Piet. His reading glasses are still by the till. The specials board is still in his handwriting. Ros wants to be asked why she has come. Nell, who has kept going by never stopping, wants her gone before either of them has to say anything. When Ros asks how she's managing, Nell says "Fine" in exactly the voice Ros uses on patients' relatives. Then Nell looks at the clock and tells her she'll want to be off, if she's going to make her shift.

Ros puts on her coat. At the door she looks up at the clock and says, "It's twenty minutes fast." Piet told her when she was ten, and swore her to secrecy: it was for the tourists. Nell realises Ros has known all afternoon that she was being hurried out, and has let herself be hurried.

Ros takes her coat off and sits down. They have twenty minutes.

In them, Nell finally asks why she came. Ros tells her she has driven to the causeway twice since the funeral and turned back both times. Today she didn't, and she can't say why. Nell tells her why she has never corrected the clock: it is the last thing in the café that is still Piet's job. Neither of them cries for long. Nell makes two more teas and, this time, doesn't charge.

When the real time comes, Ros walks back across the causeway, in good time, with the sea still well out on either side. Nell watches from the window until Ros reaches the far end and turns to wave.

The clock is twenty minutes fast. "It's right for here," says Nell. Ros tells him it has been fast since she was twelve, and nobody in the family has ever won that argument.

Between customers, mother and daughter circle the thing neither will name. Ros diagnoses the coffee machine: "It's got a murmur." Nell asks whether the hospital ever lets her sleep. "Not on purpose." They are good at being funny, and it saves them from talking.

The café empties. Howard leaves last, grumbling, in good time. Ros drags a chair to the counter to put the clock right, and Nell tells her to leave it. It becomes the argument they have both avoided, and Ros finally says it. At Piet's wake she left before it was over. She said she had to catch the tide, looked up at this clock, knew it was fast, and went anyway. She has been ashamed of it for two winters.

Nell says she knows. She watched her go. She has been waiting ever since for Ros to walk back in, and never knew how to say so on the phone.

The clock's hand touches Piet's pencil line. Ros stands and reaches for her coat, just as she did at the wake.

"Sit down," says Nell. "The clock's for visitors. You're not a visitor."

Ros sits. Nell gives her ten of Piet's twenty minutes, because he would want the other ten kept, and for the first time all day she sits down too. They don't say much. They share the last scone.

Then Ros crosses in good time, with the causeway dry and the sea still well out. Nell watches from the window until her daughter reaches the far side. Above the counter, the clock keeps its twenty minutes, as it always has.

In March last year, I spent a week at the main entrance of Orla Valley Hospital. I stood by the reception desk with a clipboard. Five days, eight in the morning until six at night. Every time someone asked one of our two receptionists a question, I wrote it down.

By the end of the week, I had thirteen hundred and twelve questions.

Three hundred and ninety of them were some version of the same question.

Where's X-ray?

On the Friday evening, I counted the signs in our main corridor. There were two hundred and fourteen. Not one of them said X-ray. There wasn't a single sign anywhere in the hospital that said X-ray.

The sign over the main corridor said Imaging and Radiology. It had said Imaging and Radiology since the building opened in 2009.

One man that week didn't ask the receptionists. He asked me. He was in a dressing gown, and he said, "Is Imaging the same as X-ray, or is that somewhere else?"

I didn't know whether it was my place to answer him.

The Monday after, we changed that one sign.

I'll come back to what happened.

# The Damp of '87

When Mum moved into Elm Court last spring, the hardest thing to find a home for was her piano. It was an upright my grandad bought second-hand in 1961, and it had been in the front room at Lark Road my whole life. Mum played it every Sunday, mostly hymns. She always said the D above middle C stuck because of 'the damp of '87', and none of us ever got round to fixing it.

I rang three dealers and none of them were interested. One of them said they're all firewood now, which I found quite upsetting.

In the end I put it on the local selling page, free to a good home, buyer collects, and a man rang that evening. He came on the Saturday with his daughter, who looked about fourteen, in a van he'd borrowed from work. She sat down with her coat still on and played a scale, and of course the D stuck. I told her what Mum always said about the damp of '87, and she laughed.

I had to go into the kitchen for a minute.

Getting it out was a whole saga. Her dad had to take the front door off its hinges, and it took the three of us nearly an hour to get it down the steps. Before they left, he gave me two twenty-pound notes, folded up small, even though the advert said free. I tried to give them back, but he wouldn't have it.

I stood on the pavement for a long time afterwards.

I kept the stool. Her music was still inside it: the Sunday hymn book, and a book of film themes I never once heard her play.

The next time I visited Mum at Elm Court, I was nervous about telling her. All she said was, 'Did the D stick?'

I said yes, and she laughed properly for the first time in months.

In March 2025, I spent a week standing by the main reception desk at Orla Valley Hospital with a clipboard.

Five days, eight in the morning until six at night. I wrote down every question people asked the two receptionists. I wasn't there to answer anything. I was there to write it down.

By the end of the week, I had one thousand, three hundred and twelve questions.

Three hundred and ninety of them were some version of "Where's X-ray?"

The sign over the main corridor said "Imaging and Radiology". It had said that since the building opened in 2009.

On the Friday evening, I counted the signs in the main corridor. There were two hundred and fourteen. And there wasn't a single sign anywhere that said "X-ray".

During that week, a man in a dressing gown came up to me instead of the receptionists. He asked me, "Is Imaging the same as X-ray, or is that somewhere else?"

I didn't know whether it was my place to answer him.

The Monday after, we changed that one sign. One sign, out of two hundred and fourteen.

I'll come back to what happened next.

# The Damp of '87

When Mum moved into Elm Court last spring, the hardest thing to deal with was her piano. It was an upright my grandad bought second-hand in 1961, and it had been in the front room at Lark Road my whole life. Mum played it every Sunday, mostly hymns. The D above middle C stuck. She always said that was "the damp of '87", and none of us ever got round to fixing it.

I was sad and guilty and cross all at once. I rang three dealers and none of them were interested. One of them said they're all firewood now. I suppose I felt like nobody understood what it meant to us.

In the end I put it on the local selling page, free to a good home, buyer collects, and a man rang that evening. He came on the Saturday with his daughter, who looked about fourteen, in a van he'd borrowed from work. She sat down with her coat still on and played a scale, and of course the D stuck. I told her about the damp of '87, and she laughed.

I had to go into the kitchen for a minute.

# The Damp of '87

When Mum moved into Elm Court last spring, the hardest thing to find a home for was her piano. It was an upright my grandad bought second-hand in 1961, and it had been in the front room at Lark Road my whole life. Mum played it every Sunday, mostly hymns. She always said the D above middle C stuck because of "the damp of '87", and none of us ever got round to fixing it.

I rang three dealers and none of them were interested. One of them said they're all firewood now, which I found quite upsetting. I suppose I felt like nobody understood what it meant to us.

In the end I put it on the local selling page, free to a good home, buyer collects, and a man rang that evening. He came on the Saturday with his daughter, who looked about fourteen, in a van he'd borrowed from work. She sat down with her coat still on and played a scale, and of course the D stuck. I told her about the damp of '87, and she laughed. I had to go into the kitchen for a minute.

Getting it out was a whole saga. Her dad had to take the front door off its hinges, and it took the three of us nearly an hour to get it down the steps. Before they left, he gave me two twenty-pound notes, folded up small, even though the advert said free. I tried to give them back, but he wouldn't have it. I stood on the pavement for a long time afterwards.

I kept the stool. Her music was still inside it: the Sunday hymn book, and a book of film themes I never once heard her play.

The next time I visited Mum, I was nervous about telling her I'd given her piano away on the local selling page. I needn't have been. All she said was, "Did the D stick?"

I said yes, and she laughed properly for the first time in months.

None of us ever did get round to fixing it.
